title: India’s Sugar Industry
subtitle: Understanding the Sector, Value Chain, and Recent Price Rise
body_text:
India’s Sugar Industry at a Glance
India’s sugar industry is a major agricultural, industrial, and rural livelihood ecosystem. India is the world’s second-largest sugarcane producer. The sugarcane sector supports nearly 5 crore farmers and around 5 lakh workers in sugar factories and its allied industries.
India’s sugarcane production has reached 500 MMT in 2025-26 as per the Third Advance Estimate of Production released by the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare. This marks approximately 43.5 percent growth over the last 10 years, compared with 348.44 MMT of production in 2015-16.
The area under sugarcane cultivation has also increased from 49.27 lakh hectares in 2015-16 to 58.87 lakh hectares in 2025-26 . Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra are the top sugarcane-producing states in India. India exported 8 lakh MT of sugar in 2025-26, compared with 0.47 lakh MT in 2016-17.
Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of sugarcane for the sugar season 2026-27 (October - September) has been set at ₹365/quintal by the government. This provides a basic recovery rate of 10.25%. This price is ₹135 more than the FRP for the sugar season 2016-17, which was fixed at ₹230/quintal with a basic recovery rate of 9.5%. Major export destinations of Indian sugar include Sri Lanka, West Asia, and East Africa . Adequate sugar buffer stocks are available, and sugar production in 2025–26 is expected to remain sufficient.
The Role of the Indian Sugar Industry in Advancing Ethanol Blending
The blending of ethanol with petrol is aimed at reducing dependence on fossil fuels and enhancing energy security. This move is in sync with the government's push for sustainable fuel alternatives.  This initiative also supports farmers by providing them with a stable income and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, this does not mean that ethanol blending would lead to a shortage in sugar for domestic consumption.
The share of sugar diverted for ethanol production has declined from around 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26. Moreover, nearly three-fourths of the ethanol produced in the country now comes from grains , particularly maize .
In fact, the ethanol programme has helped sugarcane farmers and strengthened sugar mills:
On an average, India produces around 300-340 lakh MT of sugar annually. India’s domestic sugar consumption is around 280-290 lakh MT annually. In years of surplus production, excess stocks block the funds of sugar mills and delay payments to sugarcane farmers. Diversion of excess sugar towards ethanol has helped address this structural problem and improved the financial health of sugar mills. As of August 20, 2026, 97% of sugarcane dues for the 2025-26 sugar season have already been paid to farmers. The improved financial position of sugar mills has reduced their dependence on government support. Simultaneously, retail sugar prices for consumers have also remained broadly stable, increasing by only around 3% annually between August 2024 and July 2026.
Analysing the Current Sugar Price Hike
Sugar prices have increased in recent weeks, from ₹48.18 per kg on July 20, 2026, to ₹55.70 per kg on August 20, 2026. This reflects an increase of around 15.6% within one month. It's worth distinguishing this recent movement from the longer-term trend, however: as noted earlier, sugar prices rose by only about 3% annually between August 2024 and July 2026. This suggests the current uptick largely reflects short-term supply and market factors , rather than a shift in the underlying price trend.
The present increase in sugar prices is due to a combination of factors, including:
Lower-than-expected domestic production, Increased demand ahead of the festive season, Weather-related damage to the sugarcane crop, Tightening global sugar supplies and rising prices, and Speculation and hoarding by some sections of the industry.
Sugar production during the current season is expected to be around 306 LMT , compared to the initial estimate of around 343 LMT . Production has been affected by two factors: Red Rot and Top Borer disease, and waterlogging caused by excess rainfall. However, despite the lower-than-estimated production, adequate sugar stocks are available in the country to meet domestic demand . The new crushing season will begin in October.
The tightening of sugar supplies is a global phenomenon and is not limited just to India . The global sugar deficit for 2026-27 is estimated at around 33 lakh MT. As a result, international sugar prices have risen sharply from $474/tonnes on June 30, 2026 to $552/tonnes on August 20, 2026. This marks an increase of over 16% in less than two months.
Table 1: Myth v/s Fact of Rising Sugar Prices
MYTH FACT Ethanol diversion caused the sugar price rise. Sugar diverted to ethanol production fell from 12% in 2022–23 to around 9% in 2025–26. Ethanol is taking away sugar from consumers. Nearly three-fourths of India’s ethanol now comes from grains, particularly maize. India is facing a sugar shortage. Adequate stocks are available to meet domestic demand until the new crushing season begins. Global sugar prices have remained stable. International prices rose from $474 to $552 per tonne, increasing over 16% in less than two months. India’s sugar production has collapsed. Current production is estimated at 306 LMT, below the initial estimate of 343 LMT. Sugar prices have been continuously rising sharply. Long-term prices increased by only around 3% annually between August 2024 and July 2026. Current hike price is short-term.
The government has observed that speculation and hoarding by some sugar mills and traders have also contributed to the recent price increase.
Government Efforts to Curb Hoarding of Sugar and Increase Supply
The government has taken the following steps to control the short-term price hike in sugar and curb the ongoing sugar hoarding:
A stock limit of 400 tonnes has been imposed on sugar dealers across the country from August 1, 2026, to November 30, 2026. From September 1, 2026, onwards, bulk consumers will not be permitted to hold sugar stocks exceeding 15 days of consumption. Joint teams of central and state government officials are conducting physical verification of sugar stocks at mills to check for hoarding and artificial scarcity. As a precautionary measure , the government has decided to permit duty-free import of 10 lakh MT of raw sugar to augment domestic availability. States and sugar mills have been advised to begin crushing from October 15, 2026 . This is expected to raise October sugar production from the usual 3-4 lakh MT to more than 10 lakh MT. This would improve availability during the festive season.
Looking Beyond the Current Price Rise
India’s sugar sector has evolved into a diversified industry that supports farmers, mills, energy production, and global trade. Recent price pressures reflect lower production, seasonal demand, global supply conditions, and market practices. However, these pressures remain temporary against the sector’s broader growth and diversification. The government’s priority remains balancing consumer interests, timely farmer payments, and industry stability.

enrichment.summary: This PIB backgrounder explains India's sugar industry, noting sugarcane production reached 500 MMT in 2025-26 (up 43.5% over a decade), FRP for 2026-27 set at ₹365/quintal, and clarifies that a recent 15.6% monthly sugar price spike (₹48.18 to ₹55.70/kg) is due to lower production (306 LMT vs 343 LMT estimate), festive demand, weather damage, global supply tightness, and hoarding—not ethanol diversion, which has actually declined from 12% to 9%. It also lists government measures to curb hoarding and boost supply, including stock limits, duty-free raw sugar imports of 10 lakh MT, and advancing the crushing season to October 15, 2026.
enrichment.context: Sugar is a politically sensitive commodity in India given its dual role as a food staple and a feedstock for the ethanol blending programme, which is central to India's energy security and biofuel goals (target of 20% ethanol blending, achieved ahead of schedule). The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) mechanism, administered under the Sugarcane Control Order, 1966, ensures cane growers get an assured price regardless of mill profitability, distinguishing it from the State Advised Price (SAP) some states additionally announce. Periodic sugar price volatility triggers government interventions like stock limits and export/import controls under the Essential Commodities Act, balancing farmer income, mill viability, consumer affordability, and export competitiveness. This backgrounder is significant because it directly rebuts a popular narrative (that ethanol blending is squeezing sugar supply) with data, and documents a concrete policy response (import liberalization, stock limits, crushing season advancement) to a live price crisis—both of which are examinable as current policy interventions in the agriculture-industry-energy nexus.

prelims_questions.question: With reference to India's sugar industry, consider the following statements: 1. India is the world's largest producer of sugarcane. 2. The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) for sugarcane for 2026-27 has been fixed at ₹365 per quintal. 3. The share of sugar diverted for ethanol production has declined between 2022-23 and 2025-26. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: India is the world's second-largest sugarcane producer (not largest), so statement 1 is incorrect. The FRP for 2026-27 was indeed set at ₹365/quintal, and the share of sugar diverted for ethanol fell from about 12% in 2022-23 to about 9% in 2025-26, making statements 2 and 3 correct.

prelims_questions.question: As per the PIB backgrounder on India's sugar industry, which of the following measures has the government taken to address the recent rise in sugar prices?
options: Imposing an export ban on all sugar until further notice
Permitting duty-free import of 10 lakh MT of raw sugar
Increasing the FRP retroactively for the 2025-26 season
Banning ethanol production from sugarcane entirely
prelims_questions.explanation: The government decided to permit duty-free import of 10 lakh MT of raw sugar as a precautionary measure to augment domestic availability, along with stock limits and advancing the crushing season.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the factors responsible for the recent volatility in sugar prices in India. Critically examine the effectiveness of government measures such as stock limits, duty-free imports, and advancement of the crushing season in addressing this issue.
Examine the interlinkages between India's sugarcane economy and its ethanol blending programme. How does this diversification serve the twin objectives of energy security and farmer income stability?

study_notes.reason: The release carries a solid factual core (FRP figures, the FRP-vs-SAP distinction, ethanol diversion share, stock-limit and import measures) alongside genuine analytical material (the ethanol-blending vs food-security debate, multi-causal analysis of the price spike, and the government's short-term market intervention strategy), making it a rare case where both prelims recall and mains argument-building are equally served.

prelims.point: FRP for sugarcane 2026-27 fixed at ₹365/quintal with a basic recovery rate of 10.25%, up from ₹230/quintal (9.5% recovery) in 2016-17.
prelims.why_important: FRP figures and recovery-rate linkage are a recurring objective-question theme in agricultural price policy.

prelims.point: FRP is fixed under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966 and is distinct from the State Advised Price (SAP) that some states additionally announce.
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently tests the FRP-vs-SAP distinction as a pair of easily-confused concepts in agricultural pricing.

prelims.point: Share of sugar diverted to ethanol has declined from about 12% (2022-23) to about 9% (2025-26), while nearly three-fourths of ethanol now comes from grains, chiefly maize.
prelims.why_important: Tests awareness of the shifting feedstock composition of India's ethanol blending programme.

prelims.point: India's sugarcane production reached 500 MMT in 2025-26 (Third Advance Estimate), a 43.5% rise over 2015-16's 348.44 MMT; India is the world's second-largest sugarcane producer.
prelims.why_important: A benchmark production figure and global ranking that could appear in a data-based prelims statement set.

prelims.point: Government imposed a 400-tonne stock limit on sugar dealers (Aug 1-Nov 30, 2026) and permitted duty-free import of 10 lakh MT raw sugar as short-term measures.
prelims.why_important: Specific regulatory thresholds and import quotas are the kind of scheme-parameter detail UPSC tests.

mains.point: The release explicitly rebuts the popular narrative that ethanol blending is diverting sugar and causing scarcity, using data to show diversion has actually fallen even as blending targets were met.
mains.theme: Ethanol blending vs food security trade-off
mains.analytical_use: Useful for answering questions on whether biofuel policy conflicts with food security, allowing the aspirant to present a counter-argument backed by official data rather than assumption.

mains.point: The current sugar price spike is attributed to a combination of factors - lower domestic output, festive demand, crop disease/weather damage, global supply tightness, and hoarding - rather than a single cause.
mains.analytical_use: Supports 'discuss the causes of' or 'analyse factors behind' questions on essential commodity price fluctuations, illustrating multi-causal analysis.

mains.point: Government response combined supply-side measures (stock limits, anti-hoarding verification, duty-free imports, advancing the crushing season) to manage a short-term price shock without disturbing farmer payment timelines.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for 'suggest measures' or 'evaluate government response' questions on balancing consumer affordability, farmer income and mill viability.

both.concept: Ethanol blending programme's structural role in the sugar economy - diverting surplus sugar to ethanol to prevent mills' funds being blocked, thereby improving farmer payment timeliness (97% dues paid) and mill financial health, while contributing to energy security goals.
both.prelims_angle: Could be tested on ethanol blending targets, feedstock shares, or timelines of the blending programme.
both.mains_angle: Allows analysis of the linkage between agro-industrial policy, farmer income stability, mill solvency, and energy security - a genuine cross-cutting mechanism rather than an isolated fact.

low_priority.point: Major export destinations of Indian sugar (Sri Lanka, West Asia, East Africa).
low_priority.reason: Illustrative trade detail with no independent testable or analytical value.

low_priority.point: International sugar prices rising from $474 to $552/tonne between June and August 2026.
low_priority.reason: A specific transient figure cited only to support the 'global tightening' argument, not a standalone examinable fact.

low_priority.point: 97% of 2025-26 sugarcane dues paid to farmers as of August 20, 2026.
low_priority.reason: A point-in-time administrative statistic rather than a generalizable policy fact.
